Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:6: The reason the verse calls Israel "brothers" and "fellows," saying (Leviticus 25:25), "when your brother becomes poor," and "love your fellow" (ibid. 19:18), and many similar cases, is to allude that just as a mother who bears two male children, they are called brothers because both were in the same womb, and where one was, the other was — this is the relation of brotherhood, even though the bodies are divided in their existence. The brotherhood applies even more correctly if they were born twins, both being together as one in a single womb and born as one. Along these lines there is a spiritual place above called by the designation "womb" [rechem], where the conception of souls occurs, as it says (Exodus 13:2), "sanctify to Me every firstborn, the opener of every womb" — as explained in the Zohar, portion Bereshit (13b), regarding the commandment of laying tefillin; see there. Of this it is also said (Habakkuk 3:2), "in wrath remember mercy [rachem, related to womb]" — for there, in the place of the conception of souls, six hundred thousand [souls] are in one womb and born as one; we find, then, from this aspect, that all of Israel are brothers, and it is a doubled brotherhood — since they were all as one, in one place, along the lines of twin brothers. This is a great unity for souls from the side of their spirituality. Regarding this Job said (Job 31:15), "did not He who made me in the belly make him also, and did not one [God] form us in the womb?" — mentioning two aspects, "belly" and "womb," for there are indeed these above, as it says (ibid. 38:29), "from whose belly did the ice come forth?" as my teacher, peace be upon him, explained in the Gate of the Meanings of Designations (Pardes, ch. 23, s.v. "belly").
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:7: The aspect of love from the side of the body is that he should think that since we are all shaped by a single Craftsman in His image, as it is said (Genesis 9:6), "in the image of God He made man," whoever disgraces his fellow disgraces himself. Moreover, he thereby disgraces, as it were, the Craftsman who made him. Regarding this our Sages of blessed memory said in Bereshit Rabbah (24:7): Ben Azzai says, "this is the book of the generations of man" (Genesis 5:1) — this is a great principle in the Torah. Rabbi Akiva says, "love your fellow as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) is a great principle in the Torah — that you not say, since I have been disgraced, let my fellow be disgraced; since I have been cursed, let my fellow be cursed with me. Rabbi Tanchuma said, if you do so, know whom you disgrace — He made him in the likeness of God. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:8: Further, it is explained in the Zohar (portion Miketz, 201a) that when Israel are with one another in love, they cause the side of the right and Chesed to be drawn to the world, as it is written (Jeremiah 31:2), "with everlasting love I have loved you, therefore I have drawn you with kindness [chesed]"; but if not, God forbid, the left prevails, since hatred is drawn from the left, and the external force drawn from the left is completed, and its stature becomes complete. These are his words: he opened and said, "do not say, I will repay evil" etc. (Proverbs 20:22). Come and see, the Holy One, blessed be He, made man to be strengthened in Torah and to walk in the way of truth, on the side of the right, and not to walk on the side of the left; and since they need to walk on the side of the right, they must increase love with one another, and there should be no enmity among them, so as not to weaken the right, which is the place Israel is attached to. Come and see, therefore it is [that man has] the good inclination and the evil inclination, and Israel must strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination through fitting deeds; and if a person turns to the left, then the evil inclination is strengthened over the good inclination, and whoever was deficient is completed through people's sins, for this disgraceful one [the evil inclination] is completed only through people's sins. Therefore a person must be careful that this evil inclination not be completed through his sins, and must be constantly on guard, for the good inclination wants to complete him in continual wholeness, and not the evil inclination; therefore, "do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD, and He will save you."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:9: Another interpretation: "do not say, I will repay evil," as it is written (Psalms 38:21), "and those who repay evil for good" — to one who has completed good for him, one should not complete evil for him, out of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, as in (Genesis 42:18), "do this and live" etc.; and He Himself always does so, as it is written (Proverbs 17:13), "whoever repays evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" — even if they have completed evil for him, he must not repay evil in place of the evil they completed for him, but rather, "wait for the LORD, and He will save you." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:10: Further, among the things a person should consider so as not to come to quarrel with his fellow is what the Tanna said in Avot, ch. 2 (2:4): do not judge your fellow until you reach his place. And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote in his commentary on this Mishnah, and it further seems to me, that this is a great principle for maintaining peace and love among people — for most quarrels that fall among people are caused by a person judging one standard for himself and another for another; therefore he warned, do not judge your fellow until you reach his place, and let your own mind and soul be under his soul. By way of parable: if a person disgraced you over something you did to him, do not respond to him until you yourself judge whether, had he done to you what you did to him, you would have disgraced him even more than he disgraced you. Likewise in any business dealing you have with your fellow — if you have a claim against him, consider in your mind whether, were the situation reversed, what would you want him to do with you, and equate yourself with him also. In sum, this is a great principle for increasing peace in the world. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:11: Further, one who views his fellow with a good eye will not quickly be filled with anger against him. So too the aforementioned pious author wrote regarding the Mishnah (Avot 2:10), Rabbi Eliezer says, let your fellow's honor be as precious to you as your own, and be not quick to anger — these are his words: all these warnings are a preparation for attaining wisdom, for acquiring a friend is a great aid to learning Torah, as it says, acquire for yourself a friend, and all the more so in being precise about friends. Be careful of the honor of friends, for through this their companionship will endure and they will have good reward for their labor, and in the commentary on "acquire for yourself a friend" I have written about this with Heaven's help. And as for his saying "be not quick to anger" — to me, this is because the ease and swiftness of anger correspond to the good things received by the one at whom the angry person is angry — therefore quarrels among relatives always grow greater, and the Name, blessed be He, is exacting with His pious ones to a hair's breadth, since they have received more of the true good fortune; and therefore he warned, even though you are careful about your fellow's honor and have not sinned against him while he has sinned against you, be not quick to anger. And when you examine this well, you will find this statement flowing from his own attribute, peace be upon him, which is a good eye — for one who views people with an evil eye fills his belly with people's faults, and at the slightest provocation bursts like new wineskins, as it says (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools" — because of the ease and swiftness of their anger it is as though it has made its home there; if so, the swiftness of anger reveals the shame of its possessor. But one who is slow to anger shows in his soul that he views matters with a good eye, and therefore does not quickly become angry. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:12: Further, among the things that nullify hatred and anger is the matter of rebuke — that he rebuke his fellow and say, why did you do such and such to me? And it is possible his fellow will excuse himself to him, as we find Abraham our father, peace be upon him, did with Avimelech, as it is said (Genesis 21:25), "and Abraham rebuked Avimelech concerning the well of water which Avimelech's servants had seized," and he excused himself to him, as it is said, "and Avimelech said, I do not know who did this thing" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:13: They said in Bereshit Rabbah (54:3) on this verse, "and Abraham rebuked" etc.: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina said, rebuke brings about love, as it is said (Proverbs 9:8), "rebuke a wise man and he will love you" — this is the view of Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina, who said, any love without rebuke is not [true] love. Reish Lakish said, rebuke brings about peace — "and Abraham rebuked Avimelech" — this is his view, who said, any peace without rebuke is not [true] peace. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:14: For this the Torah commanded (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him." Ramban, peace be upon him, likewise explained in his commentary on this verse, these are his words: what seems correct to me is that "rebuke you shall rebuke" is like "and Abraham rebuked Avimelech," and the verse says, "you shall not hate your brother in your heart" when he does something to you against your will, but you shall rebuke him — why did you do this to me? — "and you shall not bear sin because of him," by concealing your hatred in your heart and not telling him — for by rebuking him, he will excuse himself to you, or he will return and confess his sin, and it will be forgiven him. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:15: Since the matter of rebuke has come to us, let us say something about it, for it is a positive commandment; and first we shall copy the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, according to the plain meaning. These are his words in portion Kedoshim (85b), in the explanation of the verse: the Faithful Shepherd — this commandment is to rebuke the one who has sinned, to show him great love, so that he not be punished — for of the Holy One, blessed be He, it is written (Proverbs 3:12), "for whom the LORD loves, He rebukes"; and since the Holy One, blessed be He, rebukes whomever He loves, a person should learn from that way and rebuke his fellow. How does the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuke a person? He rebukes him with love, in private — if he accepts it, fine; if not, He rebukes him among his loved ones — if he accepts it, fine; if not, He rebukes him openly before everyone — if he accepts it, fine; and if not, He leaves him and does not rebuke him further, but lets him go and do as he wishes. First He informs him privately, in order to rebuke him and arouse him without anyone else knowing — this is between him and Him alone; if he accepts it, fine; if not, He informs him among his loved ones — at a time when the High Priest was in the world, He would send him illnesses on his bed, and the Holy One's loved ones would come and inform him whether there was a sin in him that he should repent of, and examine his words — if he accepts it, fine; if not, He rebukes him openly, through his money, through his children, since everyone whispers about him and comes to him — if he accepts it, fine; and if not, his Master lets him go and do as he wishes and never grasps hold of him again. In like manner, one must rebuke his fellow — first privately, then among his loved ones, then openly — and from then on, let him go and do as he wishes. Therefore it is written "rebuke you shall rebuke" — "rebuke" privately, so that no one else knows; "you shall rebuke" among his loved ones and companions; "your fellow" — openly. And therefore "rebuke" is not written first followed immediately by public rebuke, but rather "rebuke" then "you shall rebuke" — if the person is one who would be embarrassed, one should not tell him directly nor rebuke him even in private, but should say before him, as though speaking of other matters, and within those words mention that whoever did such a sin did such and such — so that he, knowing it applies to himself, will refrain from that sin — this is "rebuke." And if not, "you shall rebuke" — then, "your fellow" — openly; from then on, "and you shall not bear sin because of him" — for once a person rebukes his fellow and comes to rebuke him openly, he should not raise before him the actual sin he committed, for that is certainly forbidden to him, but he should speak in general terms and not raise the sin openly against him, nor mark the sin against him, since the Holy One, blessed be He, has compassion for a person's honor even among the guilty. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:16: In Arachin (16b, version cited): one might think, even if his face changes [from embarrassment, he must still be told directly] — the verse teaches, "and you shall not bear sin because of him." Rabbi Tarfon said, I am amazed if there is anyone in this generation who is able to rebuke [properly]. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said, I swear, I am amazed if there is anyone in this generation who is able to accept rebuke. Rabbi Akiva said, I swear, I am amazed if there is anyone in this generation who knows how to rebuke. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:17: In Tana d'Bei Eliyahu (Rabbah, ch. 18), copied in the Yalkut in the explanation of the verse (portion Vayikra, §613): another interpretation, [rebuke] the people who are with you regarding commandments, but do not rebuke a wicked person, lest he hate you, as it is said (Proverbs 9:7), "he who disciplines a scoffer gets himself shame" — since he is himself flawed. Thus far his words. Rabbi Elazar ben Matya said, if there is a matter between you and him, tell it to him and do not become guilty through it — for this reason it is said, "and you shall not bear sin because of him." Similarly you say (Proverbs 24:17), "do not rejoice when your enemy falls," and elsewhere it says (ibid. 11:10), "and at the destruction of the wicked, there is joyous song" — how can these two verses both be maintained? A Torah scholar who defeated you today in a matter of halakhah, and tomorrow some misfortune comes upon him — do not rejoice, lest the LORD see and it be evil in His eyes; but if you see a person in Israel who wishes ill upon his fellow, this one is a completely wicked person [and you may rejoice at his fall]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:18: In Bava Metzia (31a) it says: "rebuke" implies even a hundred times; "you shall rebuke" — I have only [learned] a teacher toward a student — from where do we learn a student toward a teacher? The verse teaches, "you shall rebuke," in any case. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:19: Regarding the reward for the one who rebukes and the one who accepts rebuke, our Sages of blessed memory said in tractate Tamid (28a), on the verse (Proverbs 24:25), "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good": it was taught, Rabbi says, what is the straight path a person should choose for himself? To love rebuke — for as long as rebuke exists in the world, contentment exists in the world, good and blessing come to the world, and evil departs from the world, as it is said, "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant." And some say, he should hold fast to extra faithfulness, as it is said (Psalms 101:6), "my eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me." Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, whoever rebukes his fellow for the sake of Heaven merits a portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Proverbs 28:23), "whoever rebukes a man, afterward finds more favor than one who flatters with the tongue," and moreover, a thread of kindness is drawn upon him, as it is said, "he finds favor." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:20: In Eleh HaDevarim Rabbah, at the beginning of the portion, these are his words: another interpretation, "these are the words" — the Rabbis say, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, since they have accepted your rebuke, you must bless them — from where do we learn this? As it is said (Deuteronomy 1:10), "the LORD your God has multiplied you" etc. And from where do we learn that whoever accepts rebuke merits blessing? For so Solomon explains, "but to those who rebuke it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good." Thus far his words. And the intent of his saying "for so Solomon explains" is to help us understand the precision of Solomon's words — for the word "upon them" [aleihem] at first glance seems superfluous if it refers back to "those who rebuke" [themselves]; therefore he explained that Solomon said "and upon them" to indicate those who accept the rebuke, who merit the blessing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:21: Further matters to be saved from anger, Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, peace be upon him, wrote in his book, these are his words: one night, on a Friday night, I was thinking about what a person should do so as not to become angry, and I began to doze off, and while dozing I felt as though someone said to me: one who wishes not to be an angry person should be a person of understanding [maskil] — meaning that he should follow the essential point of the matter and the essential content of the words, and not pay attention or heed to what his eyes see or his ears hear regarding things done or said to him to anger him, and not attend to them at all, but rather strive to focus on the essential point — meaning, on the standing of the one saying or doing them. If he sees that the one saying or doing it is a fool and a boor, his mind and the boiling of his anger will immediately cool; and if he is wise and understanding, his anger's boiling will likewise cool — for if it is a fool, he thinks about him and says, this one is a fool without sense, and his words are without understanding, and his words are nothing but the chirping of a chirping bird, or the barking of a dog, or the braying of a donkey. And regarding the wise man he thinks and recognizes that he speaks for his own good and benefit, and accepts his words and rejoices in them. He should not focus on the words said to him nor on the deeds done to anger him, but only on the standing of the one who says or does them. However, if the words or deeds are unfitting and improper, whether they come from the one who said or did them, whether wise or foolish, and someone mentions them to him — he should not focus on the one mentioning them but on the deeds themselves, since he recognizes that they are true, that he said or did them, and he will gain great benefit from this, for he will correct his own qualities.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:22: Further, I shall share good advice to ease anger and restrain it: when you have dealings with a not-good person, let there be a complete resolution in your heart to bear from him every kind of insult, in word and deed — for when a person is prepared for his fellow to insult him in word and deed, it will not come upon him suddenly and he will not become angry. He should act this way until he is free of him, and afterward flee from him like a goring ox in the month of Nissan — through this your life will be a good life. Thus far his words, though I have abbreviated it somewhat as needed for our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:23: Further, among the things that bring a person to submission and the nullification of anger, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Submission, ch. 5) that one of them is when he thinks of his own passing, that death will come to him swiftly, cutting off his desires and his hopes, and the image of him standing among the graves. The second is when it passes over a person's heart what he owes in service to God for His many kindnesses and great goodness toward him, and his own neglect of the audible and rational commandments and his shortcomings in them, and the cutting off of his excuses and pretexts on the Day of Reckoning, and his regret at the time of retribution — he should submit and break his spirit, as it is said (Malachi 3:19), "for behold, the day comes, burning like an oven" etc., "and who can endure the day of His coming" (ibid. 3:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:24: The matter of these aspects is explained in the Zohar (portion Miketz, 201b) on the verse (Genesis 43:18), "and the men were afraid because they were brought into Joseph's house." These are his words: Rabbi Yosi says, woe to people who do not know and do not consider the ways of Torah; woe to them at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to demand judgment for their deeds, when body and soul must arise to give an account of all their deeds before the spirit separates from the body — and that day of judgment is the day the books are opened and the masters of judgment stand ready, for at that time the serpent stands ready to bite him, and all his limbs are agitated toward him, and the soul separates from the body and goes wandering, not knowing which way it will go or to which place it will ascend. Woe to that day, a day of wrath and pressure, that day! Therefore a person must arouse [awe of] his inclination every day, and remember before him that day when he must stand in judgment, when they bring him under the earth to decay, and his soul separates from him. And we have learned, a person should always arouse the good inclination against the evil inclination and pursue after it — if it departs from him, well and good; and if not, he should occupy himself with Torah, for there is nothing that breaks the evil inclination except Torah; if it departs, well and good; and if not, he should remind himself of the day of death in order to break it. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:25: And he further says below: therefore a person must always be aroused by that great day, the day of judgment, the day of reckoning — for a person has nothing to shield him except the fitting deeds he does in this world, so that they shield him at that hour. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:26: When a person takes to heart that his Creator is angry with him for what he has sinned in his pride and anger, and all his deeds are written in a book, and his sin is not quickly erased, as it is written (Jeremiah 17:1), "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with the point of a diamond," as explained in the Gate of Repentance, ch. 5 — how ashamed and disgraced he will be in the future, seeing his deeds engraved before him, and how could he not be ashamed that they proclaim above, "so-and-so worshipped idols," and the other blemishes he inflicts on his own soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:27: Also, there is nothing that nullifies attachment [to God] more than anger, and therefore they said, on the day so-and-so was angry, he did not pray (Eruvin 65a). And a person's being made in the supernal image, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, means that he attaches himself to the Name, blessed be He, through the holy soul — this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 8:6), "and You have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and majesty" — this "majesty" [hadar] is the majesty of the beard, whose allusion is in a supernal place, and he says, "You have made him rule over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, all of them" etc. Through anger the soul departs from him, and what had been over everything remains beneath everything, in the kelipah, as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:28: Further, among the things that nullify anger, he wrote in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, ch. 7), that when they speak in his disgrace, if they mention a deed he actually did, he should admit his shortcoming and not go seeking excuses to clear himself and vindicate himself, as Judah said (Genesis 38:26), "she is more righteous than I." He should not strive to shame the one who reported it, nor blame him for having revealed it, but should say to him, "my brother, what you have observed of my evil deeds is nothing compared to what you do not know of me, which the Creator has extended to conceal for me — and were my evil deeds and sins revealed to you, you would flee from me." Let him submit to the Creator and thank Him for revealing to him a little of the much, to discipline him so that he return to Him. And if what was said of him is false, the one who said it loses his own merits — and it was already said of one of the pious men that people spoke ill of him, and when the matter reached him, he sent the speaker a vessel full of the choice fruit of the land, and wrote to him, "I have received that you sent me a gift from your merits, and I have repaid you accordingly." And one of the pious ones said, many people will come on the Day of Reckoning, and when their deeds are shown to them, they will find in the book of their merits, merits they never performed, and they will say, we did not do these; and it will be said to them, so-and-so did them, who spoke of you and disgraced you [thereby transferring merit to you]. Likewise, when merits are missing from the books of those who spoke in their disgrace, they will seek them at that time, and it will be said to them, they were lost from you at the time you spoke of so-and-so and so-and-so. Likewise, some will find in the book of their debts [sins], debts they did not commit, and when they say, we did not do these, it will be said to them, these were added to you because of so-and-so and so-and-so, whom you spoke against — as it is said (Psalms 79:12), "and repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom" etc. Thus far his words. Some of his words we have omitted, to avoid excessive length.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:29: Regarding this aspect of added merit that he mentioned, it seems to me that this is why David, whom Shimi ben Gera disgraced (2 Samuel 16:11), said, "leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him... perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction and the LORD will repay me good for his curse this day" — and "good" means Shimi's own merits, which will return to David in place of the curse he cursed him with.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:30: Further, among the causes that nullify anger is considering the several ruinous things that flow from anger — for one who becomes angry suddenly and does not restrain his anger comes to bloodshed, as is written in Sefer Chasidim (§655): a story of a son who greatly honored his father. The father said to him, you honor me in my lifetime; you shall honor me in my death — I command you that you delay your anger for one night and restrain your spirit so as not to speak. After his father's passing he went to a foreign country and left his wife pregnant without his knowing, and was delayed on his journey several years; when he returned to the city, he came at night and went up to the room where his wife was lying, and heard the voice of a young man kissing her; he drew his sword and wanted to kill both of them, but remembered his father's command and returned it to its sheath. He heard her say to that young man — her son who was with her — "it has been many years since your father left me; had he known a son was born to him, he would already have arranged a wife for you by now." When he heard this, he said, "open to me, my sister, my beloved — blessed is the LORD that my anger passed, and blessed is my father who commanded me to restrain my anger for a night, for I did not kill you and my son," and they rejoiced with great joy, etc. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:31: In the first chapter of Gittin (6b) our Sages of blessed memory said: Rav Chisda said, a person should never cast excessive fear within his household, for the concubine at Gibeah — her husband cast excessive fear upon her, and she caused many myriads of Israel to fall.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:32: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, whoever casts excessive fear within his household eventually comes to three transgressions: forbidden relations, bloodshed, and desecration of Shabbat. Thus far his words. And Rashi explained: forbidden relations — when the time for her immersion arrives during a cold spell, and she fears to say "I have not immersed," and has relations with him while a niddah. Bloodshed — if he strikes her, or sometimes she flees from him and falls into a pit or off a bridge. Desecration of Shabbat — sometimes she lights a lamp or cooks after dark because of her fear of him, and he does not know [it is already Shabbat]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:33: Rabbah bar bar Chana said, what our Rabbis said (Shabbat 2:7), three things a person must say in his house on Friday evening... "have you tithed? Have you prepared the eruv? Light the lamp" — one must say them gently, so that they will be accepted from him. Rav Ashi said, I had not heard this statement of Rabbah bar bar Chana, but established it on my own reasoning.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:34: Rabbi Abahu said, a person should never cast excessive fear within his household, for a great man cast excessive fear within his household — and who is he? Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel — and they [almost] fed him a limb from a living animal. Thus far. And Rashi explained that they had lost the limb from the properly slaughtered animal, and out of fear of him they cut a limb from a living animal and brought it instead, so that he would not understand [the delay]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:35: When a person considers the secret of a man and his wife in their supernal allusion — that they allude to the secret of the supernal Cherubim — when there is peace between them, they are a chariot for the supernal place, since the attribute of peace is what unifies above; and if there is no peace between them, woe to them, for they display division.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:36: In Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 11) it says, these are his words: and once He built for him a helper, a wife, he was called "ish" [man] and she "ishah" [woman]. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He placed His Name, Yah, between them — if they walk in My ways and keep My commandments, behold, My Name is placed between them and saves them from all trouble; but if not, I will remove My Name from between them, and they become fire and fire, and fire consumes fire, as it is said (Job 31:12), "for it is a fire that consumes to destruction." Thus far his words. And although this statement encompasses all commandments and all transgressions, the matter of anger in particular is the great cause of the Shechinah's departure from between them, since anger comes from the bile and liver, which is fire, as is written in Tikkunim (85a), whoever becomes angry is as though he had kindled the fire of Gehinnom; therefore, since they quarrel in anger, they become fire and fire, and it is then fire, and that fire "consumes to destruction," as Tikkunim states.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:37: Therefore the Torah commanded that a person conduct himself within his household with joy, as explained in the Zohar (portion Va'etchanan, 269), these are his words: "and you shall speak of them" — it should say "speak" [in a different form implied], but rather a person must conduct himself according to them, conducting himself so as not to stray to the right or the left; "when you sit in your house" — conducting himself in his house in the straight path and in the way of proper order that his household members learn from him, conducting himself with them calmly and joyfully, and not casting excessive fear upon his household, all his deeds in his house being in the way of proper order. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:38: One who is proud toward the members of his household is not well-received in their eyes, and the prophet Habakkuk called him "a proud man" (2:5), and so they expounded in Bava Batra (98a): Rav Yosef said, learn from this that whoever is proud, even toward the members of his household, is not well-received, as it is said, "a proud man is not at home" — in his own home.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:39: In Midrash Tehillim, on Psalm "I will sing of kindness and justice" (Psalms 101), on the verse (v. 7), "he shall not dwell within my house": Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a person must be insulted within his own house, and if within his own house he must be insulted, how much more so within the house of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:40: If his wife rebukes him regarding matters of Heaven, he is obligated to accept it from her, and this is among the ways of humility; and if she sees something in him that is not proper and does not rebuke him, she is punished — for so we find that the wife of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was punished for not having protested against him, as they said in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (18a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:41: Now, most quarrels that occur between a man and his wife are caused by the loss of money — such as when his wine or oil is spilled and the like. Regarding this they said (Ta'anit 20b) of the merit of Rav Adda, who lengthened his days because he was never exacting within his household. Likewise they expounded in Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah, portion Ki Tisa (9:2), these are their words: another interpretation, "ish ish" [man, man, doubled] — the Torah has taught you to be generous within your household: if your wine is spilled, be generous, for you will inherit [more]; and likewise your oil, "and I will fill their storehouses"; if your garment is torn, "the LORD will fill all your requests"; but if you hear your wife's word, arise like a man — to whomever you are a man [i.e., master of your own conduct], be a man — therefore it says "ish ish." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:42: Besides the fact that one who is generous with his money lengthens his days, as explained above, his sins are also atoned for — for so our Sages of blessed memory said in Sanhedrin (102b) regarding Achav: Rav Yosef said, Achav was generous with his money, and because he benefited Torah scholars from his possessions, half of his sins were atoned for him. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:43: Likewise, along these lines, if some incident occurs between one person and another in which he loses money unintentionally, if it is a small matter, he should forgive it and not drag his fellow to court over a small matter, thinking that a person does not so much as strike his finger below unless it is proclaimed above (Chullin 7b), and this is included in "sufferings," fitting to be accepted with a pleasant countenance. But if it is a matter of great loss and touches upon court proceedings, he should not soil his mouth with complaints against his fellow, handing over judgment against him, curses, and the like, but rather enter with everyone "beyond the letter of the law," as we say in the chapter "Elu Metziot" (Bava Metzia 30b): Rav Yosef taught, "and you shall make known to them" (Exodus 18:20) — this is the house of their life [livelihood]; "the way" — this is acts of loving-kindness; "in which they shall walk" — this is visiting the sick; "in it" — this is burial; "and the deed" — this is [strict] law; "which they shall do" — this is beyond the letter of the law. And he further says below: Rabbi said, Jerusalem was destroyed only because they upheld their judgments strictly by Torah law and did not act beyond the letter of the law.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:44: At the end of the chapter "HaOmanim" (Bava Metzia 83a), our Sages of blessed memory said: some porters of Rabbah bar Chanan broke a barrel of wine [belonging to him]; he seized their cloaks [as compensation]. They came and told Rav, who said to him, give them back their cloaks. He said to him, is this the law? He said to him, yes — "that you may walk in the way of good men" (Proverbs 2:20). He gave them back their cloaks. They said to him, we are poor and have labored all day and are hungry, and have nothing. He said to him, go, give them their wages. He said to him, is this the law? He said to him, yes — "and keep the paths of the righteous." Thus far his words. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained "in the way of good men" as beyond the letter of the law. When a person considers this incident, he will remove from himself, and from between himself and his fellow, and his household, much anger and quarreling that people are accustomed to be exacting about because they do not wish to act beyond the letter of the law.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:45: Even if they rob him, it is fitting that he forgive when it is impossible to bring it before judges, so that his fellow not be punished and cause the Holy One, blessed be He, to have to arrange various circumstances until the money reaches its owner's hand — along the lines of what our Sages of blessed memory explained on the verse (Deuteronomy 1:17), "do not fear any man, for judgment is God's": the Holy One, blessed be He, says, it is not enough for the wicked that they take money from one and give it to another, but they also trouble Me to return the money to its owner. Thus far his words. Yalkut, portion Eleh HaDevarim, in the explanation of the verse (§802).
